title: Gameweek 1's Biggest Fantasy Surprises
dek: Five players who blew past PitchMetric's predicted points in the season's opening round — and why a Gameweek 1 model has almost nothing to go on.
intro: Every player here cleared 30 minutes on the pitch in Gameweek 1, which leaves 229 qualifying performances to rank by one number: actual points scored minus PitchMetric's predicted points (xP) for that player, that match. The five below are the biggest positive gaps of the round — the players the model most under-rated. A shared theme runs through all five, and it's a real limitation, not a bug: Gameweek 1 is the one week of the season where nobody, anywhere, has kicked a ball yet — no goals, no assists, no minutes for any player at their current club this season. With no current-season form to go on for anyone, the model falls back to treating almost every outfield player the same: a flat floor built only from how likely their team is to keep a clean sheet, not from anything about the individual. That's exactly why it's structurally blind to the kind of breakout individual moments that decide fantasy gameweeks. See the methodology for the full model.
closing: Four of these five points came out of just two matches — Brighton's and Hull City's, both wins built on a clean sheet plus a goal from an unheralded name. That's the Gameweek 1 pattern in miniature: the model correctly rates a fixture's clean-sheet chance, but has no way yet to know which individual will supply the goal on top of it. From Gameweek 2 onward, every one of these players now has a real observed data point, and the model's individual rates stop being flat — see how that plays out in Gameweek 2's surprise list.

players.name: Maxim De Cuyper
players.analysis: The single biggest surprise of the round, in either direction. De Cuyper only signed for Brighton this summer, arriving from Club Brugge in Belgium with a real goalscoring pedigree for a full-back — 29 goals and 37 assists across his career there. None of that reputation counts for anything in a league he'd never kicked a ball in before this match, so the model had nothing to price him on beyond a bare 1.53-point floor. It was also the season's very first game, so there was no current-season form for anyone else to lean on either. He repaid the blank slate with a goal, an assist, a clean sheet and two bonus points in a 4-0 rout of Aston Villa. It wasn't a fluke on the underlying numbers either: 1.47 expected goals and 0.21 expected assists (1.68 combined) means the chances he actually got were genuinely high-quality, not scraps.

players.name: Jack Hinshelwood
players.analysis: Brighton's second Gameweek 1 shock, from the same 4-0 win over Aston Villa as De Cuyper above. Hinshelwood is a genuine homegrown talent, having come up through Brighton's own academy — but he'd never scored a Premier League goal before this match, and with it being the season's first game, there was no current-season form to separate him from anyone else in the squad either. He came off after 63 minutes with a brace, the game's top bonus haul, and 1.41 expected goals backing up the finishing — good for a predicted score of just 1.56 points, essentially the same bare floor every outfield player without a scoring history got that week. Two Brighton players this high on the same list, from the same clean sheet, says more about how little separated any two names in a squad before a ball was kicked than it does about either player individually.

players.name: Nobel Mendy
players.analysis: Hull City beat Manchester United 2-0 on their return to the Premier League, and Mendy was one of two home defenders who scored in it. Hull hadn't played a top-flight match in years before this one, so there was no recent Premier League record for Mendy or almost anyone else in the squad — the model could only lean on a generic clean-sheet floor of 1.83 points for a newly promoted side playing at home. His goal came from a shot worth only 0.28 expected goals — a low-probability strike rather than a tap-in, which makes the outcome as much a one-off as a repeatable signal. No free-licensed photo of Nobel Mendy is available on Wikimedia Commons yet.

players.name: Semi Ajayi
players.analysis: The second of two Hull City center-backs to score in that 2-0 win over Manchester United — same clean sheet as Mendy above, same 1.83-point floor, a different goal (0.52 expected goals this time, a somewhat more presentable chance). A newly promoted club with no recent top-flight matches produced two double-digit defensive returns from sixty-three shared minutes against one of the league's biggest names. There was no shame in United failing to break Hull down on the day — but nothing could have flagged in advance that it would be two Hull defenders, of all people, doing the damage at the other end.

players.name: Mamadou Sangaré
players.analysis: Two assists and a clean sheet in a 3-0 win over Spurs, from a midfielder who — like literally everyone else in the league that weekend — had no current-season form behind him yet, so the model priced him at a flat 1.95 points regardless of who he actually was. His 0.33 expected assists is the most encouraging underlying number on this list relative to the actual return — genuine chance creation, not just a stat-line that happened to him. Worth revisiting once he's built up a real run of matches for the model to actually learn from.

model_tag.html: — identical to v1 for this gameweek. There's no current-season data for anyone yet in the season opener, so v2's price-based signal has nothing to work with (what changed in v2).

title: Gameweek 2's Biggest Fantasy Surprises
dek: A Bruno Fernandes hat-trick headlines the round, but the more interesting story is what changed in the model's own inputs one gameweek in.
intro: Same method as Gameweek 1 — every player below played at least 30 minutes, and is ranked by actual points minus PitchMetric's predicted xP for that fixture. The difference this time is that the model is no longer working from a blank slate: every returning player now has one gameweek of real 2026-27 output behind their goal and assist rates, and it shows in who tops this list and why. See the methodology for exactly how a player's rate is computed from real per-match history rather than an assumption.
closing: Compare the underlying expected-goals numbers across this list and two different stories emerge. Bruno Fernandes’s 2.02 xG very nearly explains his hat-trick outright — his performance was mostly signal, a genuine chance-quality outburst the model just had no prior data to anticipate. Haaland (0.66 xG for two goals) and Groß (0.05 xG for a goal) leaned much more on finishing than on chance quality — closer to variance than to a repeatable pattern. Rayan Cherki’s case is the odd one out for a different reason: it’s the one entry on this list whose prediction has genuinely moved since we first published it, once the model stopped discarding a substitute appearance’s output outright. None of the rest is a flaw exactly — it’s what a model honestly built from observed history looks like in only its second week of data.

players.name: Bruno Fernandes
players.analysis: The biggest single surprise across both gameweeks. Fernandes played the full 90 minutes in Gameweek 1 but didn't register a goal or an assist in it — so despite years as one of the Premier League's most productive playmakers, this season had given the model nothing to go on yet, and it priced him at a generic 2.14 points, barely above a squad player's floor. What actually happened was a hat-trick plus an assist in a 5-2 win over Ipswich Town — and 2.02 expected goals means the underlying chances very nearly justify the goal tally on their own. This is the good kind of model miss: not a fluke the numbers can't explain, just one quiet opening game that happened to come right before this one.

players.name: Morgan Gibbs-White
players.analysis: Gibbs-White has been one of Nottingham Forest's most important attacking players for a couple of seasons now, and he played every minute of Gameweek 1 too — he just didn't score or set one up, so there was no current-season product for the model to price him on beyond a modest 1.72 points. Then came a goal and an assist away at Liverpool, in a match that finished 2-2, worth 13 points. The 0.79 expected goals behind his own finish is a reasonable, presentable chance rather than a wild outlier — the assist is the bigger surprise, with only 0.04 expected assists suggesting the pass that created it wasn't a high-probability chance-creation moment by the underlying numbers.

players.name: Erling Haaland
players.analysis: The most expensive player on either list, and still a double-digit surprise. Even the league's most prolific striker has games where nothing goes in — Haaland played all 90 minutes of Gameweek 1 without scoring, and with no goals on the board yet this season, the model had nothing personal to build on and started him from the same generic 2.17-point floor as everyone else. Two goals away at Crystal Palace, in the same 4-1 win as Cherki above, from just 0.66 combined expected goals is a big finishing overperformance on the underlying chances, not a case where the model missed obviously high-quality opportunities.

players.name: Rayan Cherki
players.analysis: The model's read on this one moved after we fixed a real gap: it used to count goals and assists per start only, so Cherki's 2 assists in 27 minutes off the bench in Gameweek 1 — real, meaningful output — simply didn't count toward anything, because a substitute appearance wasn't a start. Weighing by minutes actually played instead (v2, above) values that cameo as real evidence, not nothing. He started this game, played 81 minutes away at Crystal Palace in a match City won 4-1, and scored twice himself. The 0.35 expected goals behind those two finishes says this was more clinical finishing than a string of clear-cut chances — genuinely hard to have called exactly, even now.

players.name: Pascal Groß
players.analysis: Groß only returned to Brighton in January, back from a spell at Borussia Dortmund, and has quickly become the club's main penalty and set-piece taker — exactly the kind of role that can produce a goal or an assist out of nothing. None of that reached the prediction, though: he'd played the full 90 in Gameweek 1 without a goal or assist, so the model had no personal scoring history to draw on, and its 2.60-point prediction (the highest of this week's five, but driven by Brighton's own fixture rather than anything specific to him) still wasn't close to enough. Brighton conceded four goals away at Chelsea and lost 4-3, but Groß personally returned a goal and an assist worth 13 points on his own. The 0.05 expected goals behind that goal is about as low as the underlying numbers get for an actual finish — the kind of moment a box score just can't explain, whatever it looked like on the pitch.

model_tag.html: — 1 of 5 predictions revised from v1 (Rayan Cherki, below) — what changed in v2.

title: Can We Predict a Player's Market Value — and Does It Actually Tell You Anything About Fantasy Points?
dek: We built and tested three different forecasting approaches on real Transfermarkt data, plus a blended model of our own. Here's what actually predicts a player's price — and what it means for your squad.
lede: Transfermarkt's market value estimates are the closest thing football has to a public price tag. Everyone watches them — pundits use them to call transfer windows “value” or “overpaid,” and fans use them as a shorthand for “is this player good.” But can that number actually be predicted, ahead of time, from data that's already public? And if it can — does whatever predicts it also predict fantasy points?

blocks.html: We spent this research cycle finding out, using real historical data: about 187,000 valuation snapshots across roughly 9,000 players in the top five European leagues, going back to the mid-2000s.

blocks.caption: Median market value per valuation event, by league — the real data behind this research. Hover a bar for the exact figure.

blocks.text: Three different ways to forecast a price

blocks.html: We tested three well-established forecasting philosophies against each other, honestly — meaning we never let a model see the future, and we tested it both on players it already knew about (forward in time) and on players it had never seen at all.

items: Time-series forecasting. Treat a player's value history like a stock chart and extrapolate the trend. Intuitive — and it turned out to add no real predictive value at all, however carefully we tuned it. It badly underreacts when a player's trajectory bends, and wasn't even better than simply assuming a player's price won't change. We dug into exactly why (a real bug in our first attempt, then a real ceiling even once that was fixed) rather than quietly dropping it — more on that below.

Momentum. Rather than looking at one player in isolation, pool the patterns across every player: is this player's price rising fast, and is their output (goals, assists, minutes) rising too? This approach doesn't need years of history on a single player — it borrows patterns from everyone else's careers. This turned out to be the strongest of the three individual approaches.

Bayesian updating. Start with an informed opinion of what a player should be worth — anchored on their last known transfer fee, or on typical value curves for their age and league if there's no recent deal — and then update that opinion using their recent on-pitch output. The appeal isn't just the prediction itself, it's that this method also tells you how confident to be in it.

blocks.html: On top of these three, we built a fourth, blended model that combines the two strongest approaches (momentum and Bayesian updating — full details of exactly how deliberately kept behind the curtain for now) — and it beat both of its ingredients on our held-out tests, not just the weaker of the two.

blocks.text: The honest part: it's a lot easier for players you already track

blocks.html: One of the more useful things this research surfaced wasn't a number — it was a pattern. Prediction accuracy depends enormously on how much history you have on a player. For players with a rich track record, our best model's typical error was in the range of 14–15% of their value. For the full universe of players, including fringe and youth players with thin histories, that error is meaningfully higher.

We also tested the models against players they'd genuinely never seen before (not just future dates, but entirely new careers) — and here the honest picture is more encouraging than we expected going in: the models still clearly beat the simplest possible baseline (assume the price doesn't change), especially at correctly calling which direction an unfamiliar player's value is about to move. What doesn't hold up for unseen players is our blended model's edge — it's tuned for players with a track record, and a plain momentum read does just as well or better once a player is a genuine unknown. The lesson: these tools are strongest as a way to track players you're already watching forward in time — less a crystal ball for scouting a name you've never heard of, more a sharper lens on names you already follow.

blocks.text: What did fixing our mistake actually buy us?

blocks.html: Worth being honest about, since it's the most useful thing that happened in this research cycle: our first pass at the time-series approach had a real bug in how it was being tested — it made the approach look usable when it quietly wasn't. Once we caught that and re-tested everything properly, it turned out time series wasn't pulling its weight at all, however we tuned it. The honest fix was to drop it from the blend entirely and lean harder on the two approaches that actually did the work — momentum and Bayesian updating — and to sharpen the pattern-detection underneath both of them.

blocks.caption: Typical prediction error (as a % of a player's value) before and after we caught and fixed the issue — lower is better.

blocks.html: That's not a rounding error — it's roughly a 13% reduction in typical prediction error, and it came entirely from being willing to distrust a result that looked fine on the surface and dig into why. We'd rather publish the slower, more honest version of this research than the faster, flattering one.

blocks.text: What actually moves the needle — and what it means for your squad

blocks.html: Here's the part that matters most if you're playing FPL or La Liga fantasy rather than running a scouting department. We cross-referenced the features that predict market value against real Fantasy Premier League scoring data for hundreds of Premier League players. The question: does whatever predicts a rising price tag also predict fantasy points?

blocks.caption: How strongly each signal lines up with FPL points per 90 minutes, across ~500 Premier League players.

blocks.html: The single strongest signal for fantasy output wasn't market value at all — it was recent output itself. A player's trailing goal-and-assist rate correlated with their FPL points-per-90 roughly 60% more strongly than their current market value did. In plain terms: the market price is a noisier read on fantasy potential than just looking directly at what a player has actually been doing on the pitch. Value bakes in reputation, potential, and club prestige — none of which score you FPL points.

blocks.caption: Every dot is a Premier League player — hover for the name. The upward drift is the correlation above, made visible.

blocks.heading: What this means for your squad
blocks.html: Don't chase the price tag, chase the underlying output. A player whose output has quietly been trending up, before the price everyone's fixated on has caught up, is exactly the kind of gap our Transfer Finder and Predictions tools are built to help you spot.

blocks.text: Does a player's own fantasy price predict their transfer value?

blocks.html: One more thing we tried, since it's a natural question once you're staring at both datasets side by side: FPL runs its own weekly-updated "valuation" of every player — its price. That's a genuinely independent opinion of a player's worth, from a different institution, updated by a different mechanism than Transfermarkt's own valuation. Does knowing a player's FPL price, or how many fantasy points they've racked up recently, help predict where their transfer value is headed?

Short answer: not really, and the reason is a nice bit of intuition once you see it. FPL price is deliberately compressed for game balance — two squad players can cost the same in FPL while being worth wildly different amounts on the transfer market. It just isn't fine-grained enough to track real value differences. Recent fantasy points fared a little better on their own, but added almost nothing once our model already knew a player's actual output (goals, assists, minutes) — it was measuring mostly the same thing through a different lens. A tidy negative result, but a real one, and exactly the kind of thing worth checking rather than assuming.

This is the first entry in our new Deep Research series — periodic, honest, methodologically serious dives into questions we're genuinely curious about, using real data and real held-out testing rather than vibes. Part of that honesty: an earlier pass at this analysis had a real mistake in how the time-series approach was being evaluated, and fixing it (rather than quietly deleting the disappointing result) is exactly what led us to the stronger blended model above. We'll keep that habit up — next on the list is validating our blend against players our models have never touched at all, and seeing whether a smarter time-series approach can add anything once it's given a fairer shot.
If you want the numbers behind your own squad, head to Transfer Finder or Predictions — both are built on the same “trust the underlying output” philosophy this research validated.

title: Does Blending In Price and Squad Depth Actually Improve Our Predictions?
dek: We shipped an update that leans on a player’s price and squad standing when their own track record is thin. Then we backtested it against a full season, gameweek by gameweek, and held players out entirely to check we weren’t just fitting noise. One idea didn’t survive contact with the data — here’s what we found, and what we reverted before it really shipped.
lede: A few days ago we described, in plain terms, an update to how PitchMetric prices players who don’t have much of a current-season track record yet — leaning more on what their price and squad standing already imply, fading out as real form takes over. That’s a reasonable-sounding story. It’s also exactly the kind of claim that should be tested against real results before anyone trusts it, so that’s what this post is: a proper backtest, not a victory lap.

blocks.html: We reran the update, gameweek by gameweek, across the entire 2025-26 Premier League season — 37 separate tests, each one predicting a gameweek using only the information that would genuinely have been available before it (no hindsight, no rerunning history with the benefit of knowing what actually happened). Alongside that walk-forward test, we ran a second, stricter check: for several gameweeks, we split the players who inform the price-based part of the model into groups, rebuilt that part of the model with entire groups of players excluded, and scored predictions only for the players who’d been excluded — the closest thing to testing on players the model has genuinely never seen.

Averaged across the full season, the updated model’s prediction error came down by about 3% against the version it replaced. Not enormous — but real, and worth digging into where it actually came from, because the average hides a much more interesting pattern.

blocks.caption: Prediction-error reduction (lower error is better), grouped by how much current-season history a player actually had going into that prediction.

blocks.html: The gain is concentrated almost exactly where it was designed to be, and fades out to almost nothing everywhere else. A player with no current-season track record yet saw the single biggest error reduction of the season — about 15%. By the time a player has six or more matches of real evidence behind them, the improvement shrinks to under 1%. That fade is the point, not a disappointment: if the price-based estimate were still moving the needle for well-established players, that would be a sign it was fighting a player’s actual form for influence, not filling in for its absence.

blocks.text: The honest part: one piece of this didn’t survive testing

blocks.html: The update we tested here originally had a third component too: a short-term “momentum” adjustment, nudging a prediction up or down based on whether a player’s recent form was running hotter or colder than their season average. It’s an intuitive idea. It’s also exactly the kind of idea that’s easy to talk yourself into without checking — so we checked.

blocks.caption: Prediction-error reduction for established players only (6+ matches of history) — negative means the error got worse, not better.

blocks.html: For players with little history, momentum barely moved anything either way — there isn’t enough recent form yet for a “recent vs. average” comparison to mean much. But across the roughly 90% of a season where most players already have a real track record, adding momentum made predictions measurably worse, not better — enough to wipe out more than the gain everything else in the update was providing on its own. Short-term hot and cold streaks in football are famously noisy, and a model that reacts to them mostly ends up reacting to the noise, not the signal. We pulled it before it shipped in anything but this test.

blocks.heading: The same lesson, twice now
blocks.html: This is close to the exact same lesson our first Deep Research post landed on, with a completely different question: an intuitive-sounding idea that doesn’t survive being tested honestly is worth more to know about than one that quietly ships because nobody checked.

blocks.text: Does it generalize, or did it just memorize its own training data?

blocks.html: A model that only works well on the exact players used to build it isn’t actually learning a general relationship — it’s just curve-fitting. So for several gameweeks across the season, we rebuilt the price-based part of the model multiple times per gameweek, each time with a different slice of players entirely removed from what it was allowed to learn from, and then scored it only on the players it had just been denied.

blocks.caption: Mean absolute prediction error (fantasy points), same population of players in all three bars — only which players informed the price-based estimate differs.

blocks.html: The gap between “players used to inform the price-based estimate” and “players it had never seen at all” is small enough to be noise. That’s the result we wanted: it means the price-based estimate is learning something genuinely general about how price relates to output, not memorizing the specific players who happened to train it.

Momentum as a short-term recency multiplier didn’t hold up — that doesn’t mean recent form is worthless, only that our first attempt at capturing it wasn’t. A more careful, properly-lagged version of the same idea is worth another look before we write it off entirely. We’re also keeping an eye on whether the price-based estimate’s benefit holds up the same way once a second season of results exists to test it against — one season, however thoroughly tested, is still one season. If you want to see the current model in action, Predictions and Transfer Finder are both running on exactly what’s described here — and see Methodology for the plain-language version of how it all fits together.

title: Gameweek 3's Biggest Fantasy Surprises
dek: Two of this week's five biggest surprises came from the exact same match — one from each side. The first surprise post built entirely on our updated model.
intro: Same method as Gameweeks 1 and 2 — every player below played at least 30 minutes, ranked by actual points minus PitchMetric's predicted xP for that fixture. This is the first list built entirely on the updated model — though as it turns out, the update's headline piece (leaning on price when there's not much track record yet) still hasn't had real players to work with this early in the season; it needs a few matches' worth of established players before it can learn anything, and nobody's quite there yet. What's below instead reflects the model's fixture-level read, or the same minutes-not-starts fix already visible in last week's Cherki case. One honest caveat: Gameweek 3 hadn't been officially finalized by FPL at the time of writing (bonus points can shift slightly in the day or two afterward), so treat the numbers below as very likely final rather than certainly final.
closing: Brighton's home draw with Leeds produced two of these five on its own, from opposite ends of the same ninety minutes — proof that “surprise” doesn't mean the model was clueless about the match, just wrong about a specific name within it. Compare that to Isak's case: the least surprising kind of surprise, a proven talent simply having a very good day against a prediction that already knew he was decent, just not decent enough to see two goals coming.

players.name: Jayden Bogle
players.analysis: The single biggest surprise of the round, and one that isn't really about Bogle personally at all — it's a fixture-level miss. Leeds went away to a Brighton side that had just put four past Aston Villa and beaten Manchester United, and the model's underlying read gave a Leeds defender very little credit for keeping anything out that day. Bogle, an established first-choice right-back rather than an unknown quantity, broke that read on his own: he scored, and personally kept a clean sheet for the 60 minutes he was on the pitch, before Brighton's equalizer arrived after he'd already been substituted, in a match that finished 1-1. The model had a real opinion here — it was just wrong.

players.name: Tyrick Mitchell
players.analysis: An established regular at left-back for Palace, not someone the model had no history on — the surprise here is the kind of return, not the player. Palace won 3-2 away at Fulham with both sides trading goals throughout, and Mitchell personally scored twice at the other end of a game his own team conceded two in — no clean-sheet bonus propping this one up, just pure goal threat from a full-back. Attacking returns from a defender, however established, are inherently harder for a model built on clean-sheet probability and a player's usual scoring rate to see coming than defensive ones are.

players.name: Harvey Barnes
players.analysis: An established Newcastle winger with a real track record, who simply had an excellent day at exactly the moment the model wasn't banking on one: a goal and an assist at home in a 2-2 draw with Bournemouth, worth 12 points against a 1.53 prediction. Nothing structurally unusual about this miss — just good, in-form football beating a modest, evidence-based baseline on the day.

players.name: Luka Vušković
players.analysis: The same Brighton-Leeds match as Bogle above, seen from the other side. Vušković is a brand-new arrival at Brighton — a club-record transfer worth up to £50m from Tottenham this summer, after a breakout loan season at Hamburg that won him the Bundesliga's Rookie of the Year award — so there's a real, defensible reason the model had comparatively little of his own to go on, on top of how tough it read the fixture for either side that day. His goal proved to be Brighton's equalizer, canceling out Bogle's earlier one for Leeds in a match that finished 1-1. Two of this week's five biggest surprises, from a combined 150 minutes of the same game.

players.name: Alexander Isak
players.analysis: Isak needs no introduction as a talent — Liverpool paid a British transfer record (£125m) for him roughly a year before this season kicked off — but reputation alone was never what fed this prediction. What mattered is that after a blank in Gameweek 1, he'd already opened his account with a goal in Gameweek 2, and that real, if thin, current-season record is what the model was actually working from: 3.77 points predicted, well above a total unknown's floor. He doubled up with a brace away at Ipswich Town in a 2-0 win, worth 13 points. At just 0.21 combined expected goals for two actual finishes, this was clinical finishing well ahead of the underlying chance quality — the smallest, most ordinary kind of surprise on this list: a proven forward simply having a very good day.

title: Is High Pressing Actually Taking Over Football? Five Seasons of Data From Europe's Top Five Leagues
dek: “Everyone presses now” is one of modern football's most repeated claims. We pulled team and player event data across the Premier League, La Liga, Bundesliga, Serie A and Ligue 1 to actually test it — and the honest answer is more interesting than a straight yes.
lede: Commentators have been saying it for a decade: the modern game presses harder, higher, and more relentlessly than ever, and possession football is on the way out. It's a good story. We wanted to know if it's a true one — not the vibe, the actual numbers, tested for statistical significance rather than eyeballed off a couple of famous teams.

blocks.html: So we built a dataset: team and player-level defensive-pressure event counts, possession shares, and final league standings across all five of Europe's traditional top leagues, covering as many recent seasons as we could reliably get real data for. Then we asked four specific questions — is pressing volume actually rising, has it come at the expense of possession, does it look different for rich clubs than poor ones, and what's the actual role forwards play in it — and let the data answer each one on its own, even where that meant walking back the premise.

Team-level defensive-pressure event data (the “Pressures” stat behind most of this piece) comes from a public research mirror of a well-known football-stats site, sourced from event-tracking data. That provider changed hands industry-wide in October 2022, and pressure-event counts specifically stopped being published in our source from the 2022/23 season onward under the new provider's different tracking methodology. Rather than splice two incompatible counting methods into one line and pretend it's a clean trend, we've scoped the pressing-specific analysis to the five full seasons where the same counting method applies throughout: 2017/18 through 2021/22, roughly 490 team-seasons across the five leagues. Possession shares and league tables don't have this problem, so those extend one season further, through 2022/23.

blocks.heading: Why we're not just re-scraping past October 2022
blocks.html: The site itself blocks automated access outright, and re-building years of positional/event data from scratch wasn't realistic for this piece. We'd rather publish five clean, honestly-sourced seasons than stretch a shakier one on top and let a data-provider switch masquerade as a tactical trend — that mistake alone would make a fascinating (wrong) headline.

blocks.text: Is the total volume of pressing actually rising?

blocks.html: Short answer: no — if anything, it's gone slightly the other way. Averaged across all five leagues, the number of defensive-pressure events per 90 minutes peaked in 2018/19 and was lower in 2021/22 than it was at the start of our window.

blocks.caption: League-average defensive-pressure events per 90 minutes, all five top leagues pooled, 2017/18–2021/22 (n≈490 team-seasons). 2020/21's dip lines up with the Covid-disrupted, fixture-congested season — but the overall five-season slope is still a statistically significant decline, not just that one year.

blocks.html: Running a straight regression of press events per 90 against season year, pooled across all ~490 team-seasons, gives a slope of −2.5 events/90 per season (r = −0.24, p = 7×10−8) — small in absolute terms, but about as far from statistical noise as this kind of data gets. It isn't one outlier league dragging the average down, either: four of the five leagues show their own significant downward slope on their own.

blocks.caption: Per-league trend in pressure events per 90, in events/90 per season, 2017/18–2021/22. Four of five leagues decline significantly; Ligue 1 is the one league where the five-season slope isn't distinguishable from flat.

blocks.html: If your mental model of “the pressing revolution” is more of it, every year, everywhere — that's the part of the popular story the data doesn't support, at least not in raw event-count terms.

blocks.text: But raw volume is hiding two real, and more interesting, trends

blocks.html: Total volume falling doesn't mean nothing changed. Two things move in the opposite direction, and both are statistically real:

items: Pressing is getting more efficient. The share of pressure events that actually win the ball back rose from 28.6% in 2017/18 to 29.9% in 2021/22 (slope +0.53 points/season, p = 1×10−13).

What pressing remains is shifting higher up the pitch. The share of a team's pressure events happening in the attacking third — as opposed to their own defensive or middle third — rose from 21.5% to 23.4% over the same five seasons (p = 2×10−7). Attacking-third pressing volume itself is roughly flat (p = 0.09, not quite significant) even while total volume falls, meaning teams are cutting pressing everywhere except up near the opponent's goal.

blocks.caption: Two real five-season trends hiding inside a falling total: pressing has become more concentrated near the opponent's goal, and more likely to actually win the ball, even as the raw event count declines.

blocks.html: Put together, the honest one-line summary isn't “pressing is rising” — it's pressing is getting smarter, not more frequent: less pressing overall, concentrated where it does the most damage, and landing more often when it happens.

This one needs care, because league-average possession is mechanically stuck near 50% — it's zero-sum within any match, so an aggregate “did average possession fall over time” test is meaningless by construction (and, confirming that, our five-league average sits at 50.0–50.1% every single season). The real question is a cross-sectional one: within a season, do the teams that press more tend to be the teams with less of the ball?

blocks.caption: Every team-season in the dataset: possession share vs. pressing volume (n = 490, all 5 leagues, 2017/18–2021/22). Correlation r = −0.39, p = 5×10<sup>−19</sup> — real, but far from a tight line, which is itself the point: plenty of teams with modest possession press relatively little, and vice versa. Hover a point for the club and season.

blocks.html: That relationship is real and fairly strong: r = −0.39 (p = 5×10−19). Teams with less of the ball do press more — which is exactly what you'd expect mechanically (you can only press when you don't have the ball, so less possession simply means more time available to do it), as much as it reflects a deliberate tactical choice. Where it gets more interesting is asking which style actually works.

series.label: Correlation: pressing volume ↔ points per game

blocks.caption: How strongly each style metric correlates with points per game, season by season. Possession's link to winning has stayed strongly positive throughout (all p < 10⁻¹³); pressing volume's link has stayed negative and, if anything, gotten more so by 2021/22 (p = 1×10⁻⁸).

blocks.html: So: no, pressing hasn't replaced possession as the winning recipe — quite the opposite, on this data. Teams that keep the ball more still win more, consistently, every one of the five seasons we tested. Teams with high total pressing volume tend to have fewer points, not more, and that gap has widened rather than closed. That sounds like it contradicts the “elite pressing team” image (Liverpool under Klopp, Manchester City's own counter-press) — until you separate where the pressing happens, which is the next section.

blocks.text: Rich clubs, poor clubs, and where pressing actually happens on the pitch

blocks.html: We split teams two ways — by final league position (top/middle/bottom third of the table, all five leagues, all five seasons) and, for the Premier League specifically, by total squad market value (bottom/middle/top third by transfer-market valuation, using Transfermarkt data hand-matched to club names). Both cuts tell the same story, independently.

blocks.caption: Where pressure events happen on the pitch, by final-table tercile (all 5 leagues, 2017/18–2021/22). A zone-based proxy for a pitch heatmap — we have defensive/middle/attacking-third counts, not raw x/y coordinates, so this shows the pitch-third split rather than a true positional heatmap.

blocks.html: Bottom-third teams actually generate more total pressure events than top-third teams (156 vs 147 per 90) — but nearly all of that extra volume sits in their own defensive third (55 vs 45 per 90). Top-third teams press less overall, but more of what they do happens in the attacking third (36 vs 32 per 90). In plain terms: for a struggling side, most of what shows up in the stats as “pressing” is really just defending under siege deep in their own half — not the front-foot, opponent's-box gegenpress associated with the elite sides.

The Premier League squad-value cut lands in exactly the same place, independently sourced: teams in the bottom third by squad market value (average €186m) pressed more overall (157 events/90) than the top third (average €804m, 144 events/90), had far less of the ball (44.7% vs 58.0% possession), and pressed less in the attacking third specifically (33.0 vs 35.6 events/90). Across the whole sample, squad value correlates strongly with possession (r = 0.79, p = 5×10−22), negatively with total pressing (r = −0.43, p = 8×10−6), and positively with attacking-third pressing specifically (r = +0.25, p = 0.01).

blocks.heading: “High pressing” is really two different things
blocks.html: Football media uses one phrase for two different behaviors that show up almost as opposites in the data: a rich, dominant side stepping up and squeezing you high in the attacking third, and a struggling side dropping deep and defending for their lives in their own third. Both generate “pressure events.” Only one of them is what people usually mean when they say a team “presses.”

blocks.text: Forwards' role in the press — and how it's shifted

blocks.html: Forwards do the most attacking-third pressing of any position group by a wide margin — unsurprising, since it's the zone they already occupy — averaging 6.1–6.6 attacking-third pressure events per 90 across the five seasons, versus 1.6–1.9 for everyone else combined (defenders, midfielders and goalkeepers pooled, most of whom rarely operate that high up the pitch by design). The more interesting question isn't the gap — it's how forwards' share of that team-wide effort has moved.

series.label: Forwards' share of team's attacking-third pressing

blocks.caption: What share of a team's total attacking-third pressure events came from players listed at forward, by season. Down from 64% to 59% — a statistically significant decline (p = 3×10⁻⁶).

blocks.html: Forwards went from generating roughly two-thirds of their team's high pressing to a little under three-fifths of it (p = 3×10<sup>−6</sup>) — not because forwards are pressing less individually (their own per-90 rate is statistically flat across the five seasons, p = 0.53), but because everyone else's is rising: non-forwards' attacking-third pressing rate climbed significantly over the same window (p < 0.001). The high press hasn't become a forwards' job that's intensified — it's become a whole-team structural job that midfielders and even defenders are being asked to share in more than they used to.

blocks.text: How the top five leagues compare

blocks.caption: Average defensive-pressure events per 90, 2021/22 (the last season our source has a like-for-like count for). The Bundesliga's press-heavy reputation — the Klopp/Nagelsmann/RB Leipzig lineage — holds up as the real top-line number, with La Liga's more patient, possession-first tradition sitting at the other end.

Pitch-zone share of each league's pressing, 2021/22 — the same zone-proxy heatmap as above, split by league. The Premier League and Bundesliga send the largest share of their pressing into the attacking third (≈23.9% each); La Liga sends the least (22.5%) and defends the most in its own third instead.

blocks.text: What this data can't tell us

items: Event-count pressing stats (how many times a player closes down an opponent) are a real signal, but they're a coarser tool than a true positional-tracking metric like PPDA (passes-per-defensive-action) or genuine x/y heatmaps — neither of which we could reliably access for this piece. What's here measures how often teams press and roughly where, not the full coordination and intensity a coaching staff would look at.

The squad-value “rich vs poor” cut is Premier League-only — name-matching Transfermarkt valuations to the other four leagues' club names by hand wasn't practical for this cycle, though the table-position cut (which covers all five leagues) points the same direction independently.

This is a research post, not a model change — nothing here feeds PitchMetric's actual predictions today. If a reliable, current cross-league pressing feed becomes available, a team's pressing profile is a plausible future input to how we think about defensive difficulty; that's not built, and this post isn't claiming it is.

blocks.html: The honest summary: “pressing is taking over” is a catchier headline than what the last five full seasons of data actually show. Total pressing volume is flat-to-down, not up. Possession still predicts winning better than pressing does, and that gap hasn't closed. What has genuinely changed is more specific and more interesting than the popular version — pressing has gotten more efficient, concentrated closer to the opponent's goal, and spread out across more of the team rather than resting on the forwards alone. See Methodology for how PitchMetric's actual predictions work, and the rest of the blog for our other research posts.
